detailed_results.reply:
With 500 ha and $50,000 of cash in Iowa, plus 500 t of storage, the shadow price of one extra tonne of storage is **$0 per tonne**. Storage is not binding: the optimal plan leaves the silo empty, so extra capacity would add nothing.

The other shadow prices in this scenario are:
- Land: $0 per extra hectare
- Own capital: $0.85 per extra dollar
- Credit line: $0.79 per extra dollar

On the storage economics:
- **Corn**: harvest net price $139.67/t; break-even to store in your own silo until June 2027 is $159.60/t versus a model end net price of $159.83/t — so corn does pay to store.
- **Soybean**: harvest net price $386.19/t; break-even is $414.33/t versus a model end net price of $398.96/t — so soybean does not pay to store.

detailed_results.text: If post-harvest monthly price rise is 2% instead of default on 500 ha with 1000 t storage in Iowa, what is the NPV?
detailed_results.reply:
**NPV with a 2% post-harvest monthly price rise: about 171,881 USD** (in April 2026 dollars), on your 500 ha in Iowa with 1000 t of storage.

The important finding: **the higher price rise does not change the plan at all.** The optimal solution still stores nothing:

- The 1000 t silo stays empty (peak stock 0 t), so storage is worth **0.0 USD/t** at the margin.
- All **719.7 t of soybean** are sold at harvest in November — none is held for the higher later prices.
- Only **175.5 ha** are sown (all soybean); **324.5 ha are left unsown**.

Why raising the monthly price rise from the default to 2% has no effect: storing grain costs you 2.0 USD/t/month, and the plan is limited by working capital, not by storage or by the price curve. Holding grain would tie up cash that earns more elsewhere in the plan, so selling at harvest stays optimal even with a steeper price curve.

One caveat worth knowing: this result is specific to your current setup (500 ha, 1000 t of storage, own capital and credit line as assumed in the scenario). If you'd like, I can check what would have to change for storing to pay — for example a lower storage cost, a bigger credit line, or a different crop mix.

detailed_results.text: I want to plant on -50 hectares with $50,000 cash in Iowa.
detailed_results.reply:
No he podido armar el escenario: **-50 hectáreas no es un área válida**. El motor exige un área entre 1 y 100,000 ha.

Los parámetros correctos serían:
- `area_ha`: número de hectáreas (positivo)
- `own_capital_usd`: 50,000 (su capital propio)

¿Me confirma cuál es el área real que quiere sembrar? Por ejemplo, ¿quería decir **50 hectáreas** (y no -50)? Con eso armo el escenario para Iowa con $50,000 de capital y le devuelvo el plan óptimo.

detailed_results.text: En 500 ha en Pergamino con 50 lucas, ¿cuánto me come el flete interno en porcentaje?
detailed_results.reply:
Con las 500 ha en Pergamino y los USD 50.000 de capital propio, el flete interno —de la tranquera al puerto de Rosario— es de 16,5 USD por tonelada, y en el plan óptimo representa el 5,6% del valor de la producción.

Lo que te cuesta por cultivo, comparando el precio de pizarra en puerto con el que te queda puesto en el campo:

- Trigo: de 202,97 a 186,47 USD/t
- Maíz: de 176,13 a 159,63 USD/t
- Soja: de 357,76 a 341,26 USD/t
- Girasol: de 407,88 a 391,38 USD/t

En todos los casos son los mismos 16,5 USD/t, así que el peso relativo es mayor en los granos de menor precio por tonelada (maíz y trigo) y menor en soja y girasol. Tené en cuenta que ese flete ya viene incluido en el costo de comercialización de la fuente, así que se cuenta una sola vez.
